intro: Two boxes of cereal sit on a shelf. One costs less. The other holds more. A ten-dollar bill sits in your hand after a morning of yard work. Friends are going for pizza, and there is a bike in a shop window. These are money choices, and people make them every single day. This unit is about making them on purpose.

First you will learn that a price is only half an answer. You will find the unit price by dividing, read the small tag on the shelf, and decide when the big box really is the better deal. You will compare a store brand to a name brand, test a coupon with math, sort needs from wants, and write a list that keeps you on budget.

Then you will follow money from a job to a goal. You will keep a record of what you earn, put savings in one place you can see, and figure how many weeks until the goal. You will learn what a bank does and what interest is, and you will split money into spend, save and share. By the end, you will be able to plan every dollar.
bigQuestion: How do you get the most from the money you have, now and later?

timeline.t: People trade goods directly, a basket of grain for a pair of sandals, before money is common
The United States sets up its Mint and makes the dollar the nation's unit of money
The U.S. government issues its first paper money during the Civil War
Congress creates the Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States
King Kullen opens in New York and is often called the first American supermarket
Federal deposit insurance begins, protecting money people keep in banks
Sylvan Goldman introduces the shopping cart in his Oklahoma City stores
Diners Club issues one of the first charge cards, a step toward modern credit cards
One of the first automated teller machines in the United States opens in New York
Some states begin requiring stores to show unit prices on shelf tags
A pack of gum in Troy, Ohio becomes the first item scanned with a bar code at a checkout
Shoppers compare unit prices and use coupons on phones, and kids open savings accounts with a parent

words.d: the amount of money you pay for something; only half the answer
the cost of one unit, such as one ounce, found by dividing price by amount
the small label on the shelf edge that shows the price and often the unit price
a product sold under the store's own name, usually for less than a name brand
a paper slip or phone code that takes a set amount off one item's price
something a person must have to live and stay healthy, like food and shelter
something nice to have but not needed to live
to get money in return for work you do
something you decide to work toward, like saving $120 for a bike
money you put into a bank account
money a bank adds to your savings for keeping your money there
a written plan that gives every dollar coming in a place to go

test.q: A $3.00 bag holds 2 pounds and a $4.00 bag holds 5 pounds. Why is the $4.00 bag the better deal?
choices: It is on the top shelf
test.why: $4.00 for 5 pounds is 80 cents a pound; $3.00 for 2 pounds is $1.50 a pound.

test.q: How do you find a unit price?
choices: Multiply the price by the amount
Divide the price by the amount
Add the price and the amount
Read the front of the box
test.why: Unit price is price divided by amount.

test.q: A 64-ounce bottle costs $3.20. What is its unit price?
test.why: 320 cents divided by 64 is 5 cents per ounce.

test.q: One tag says cents per ounce and the next says cents per pound. What must you do?
choices: Change them to the same unit first
test.why: You can only compare unit prices in the same unit; 16 ounces make a pound.

test.q: A 6-pack of yogurt is 50 cents a cup and a 12-pack is 60 cents a cup. Which is the better buy?
test.why: The lower unit price, 50 cents per cup, is the better deal even though the pack is smaller.

test.q: Where do you check whether a store brand has the same things in it as a name brand?
test.why: The ingredient list names everything in the food.

test.q: A $3.00 box has a 60-cent coupon. What do you pay?

choices: A second coat in a new color
test.why: Clothes for the weather are a need; the others are wants.

test.q: Why should a shopping list follow the store's layout?
choices: You walk the store once and do not go back
test.why: A list in store order means one trip through the aisles.

test.q: Three lawns at $10 each, minus $4 spent on bags. What did you keep?
Your goal is $120 and you save $20 a week. How many weeks?

choices: Money you take out of a bank
Money you put into a bank account
test.why: Deposits go in; withdrawals come out.

test.q: $100 saved at 2 percent for one year earns how much interest?
$10 comes in. Spend gets $5, save gets $3. How much goes to share?
In a balanced budget, what does money out add up to?
test.why: Every dollar of income gets a job, and the parts add up to the total.

write.prompt: Plan a shopping trip for one meal with a $15.00 budget (example prices are fine). Write the list in store order with an amount for each item, pick between two sizes or brands of one item using unit price, and show your running total. Then explain why each step is there.
tips: Start the list at the cupboard: what do you already have?
Put the items in the order of the store, frozen food last.
Show the division for the unit price and say which one wins.
Add the running total and check it against $15.00.
Sort each item into need or want and say why.
